Figure 1:Overview of coverage-aware evidence-to-action evaluation in E2A-Bench.
Existing evaluations are often coverage-blind and chain-blind: they measure whether claims are supported, but not whether models preserve actionable coverage or maintain full-chain reliability.E2A-Benchaddresses both by evaluating evidence-to-action reliability through grounding, coherence, calibration, and net decision reliability.

Figure 2:Evidence-to-action scoring protocol inE2A-Bench.
A model response is parsed into claims, rationale polarity, action, and confidence; claims are verified against deterministic OHLCV evidence anchors; and the response is scored along grounding, reasoning–action consistency, evidence–confidence calibration, and directional coverage.

Figure 3:Example of evidence-to-action scoring.
Given a chart-only query, the VLM produces a technical analysis, rationale, action, and confidence score, which are parsed and verified against deterministic OHLCV evidence anchors.
Here, a high-confidenceSELL\mathrm{SELL}recommendation has coherent reasoning but contains two unsupported claims and insufficient evidence for its confidence, yieldingUCR=0.50\mathrm{UCR}=0.50,RCI=0\mathrm{RCI}=0,ECI=1\mathrm{ECI}=1, andNDR=0\mathrm{NDR}=0.

Figure 4:Input modality effects on baselineNDR.(a)Model-wiseNDRacross text-only, chart-only, and multimodal inputs for 12 representative models.(b)MeanNDRby modality across all 20 evaluated models, with95%95\%bootstrap confidence intervals.
Modality effects are model-dependent; chart-only input achieves the highest average baselineNDRacross the full model set.

Figure 6:Coverage trap in claim-level hallucination evaluation.
Gemma-4-E2B-It avoids verifiable technical claims and outputs a non-directionalHOLD\mathrm{HOLD}decision, yielding zero observedUCRbut no actionable coverage.
In contrast, Qwen3.5-4B issues a directionalSELL\mathrm{SELL}recommendation whose claims are supported by the evidence anchors.
This case illustrates why claim-level hallucination scores alone can overestimate conservative non-action, whileNDRdistinguishes non-action from evidence-backed decision reliability.

Figure 8:Final-action distribution over 55,209 successfully parsed actions.HOLD\mathrm{HOLD}andUNCERTAIN\mathrm{UNCERTAIN}account for 63.6% of parsed actions, motivating coverage-aware evaluation beyond claim-level hallucination.

Figure 11:Local diagnostics capture non-redundant failure modes.
The heatmap reports pairwise Spearman correlations amongUCRdir\textsc{UCR}_{\mathrm{dir}},RCI, andECIacross 20 models.
All off-diagonal correlations are small (ρ≤0.26\rho\leq 0.26), indicating that factual grounding, reasoning–action consistency, and evidence–confidence calibration measure largely distinct aspects of evidence-to-action reliability.

Figure 12:Imperfect claims can still yield reliable action.
Qwen3.5-4B makes one unsupported claim, resulting in non-zeroUCR, but itsSELL\mathrm{SELL}action remains directionally covered, coherent with the bearish rationale, and supported by multiple verified evidence signals.
This example shows thatNDRis not a perfection-based hallucination score; it evaluates whether an actionable recommendation remains sufficiently evidence-backed across the full chain.
